title: Transport in Humans
seo_title: Secondary 3 Biology: Transport in Humans Worksheets (O-Level 6093 with Answers)
standard_text: Describe the components of blood and their functions, including the roles of phagocytes, lymphocytes and platelets and the process of blood clotting; describe the structure and function of the heart, the cardiac cycle and double circulation; relate the structure of arteries, veins and capillaries to their functions; describe the formation of tissue fluid; describe coronary heart disease and the factors that increase the risk (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Biology 6093 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Biology worksheets on transport in humans: blood, clotting, the heart, double circulation, arteries, veins, capillaries, cardiac output and coronary heart disease. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Arteries away, veins back to the heart.
key_sub: The left ventricle has the thickest wall: it pumps to the whole body.
body_html:
How to think about it

Blood goes through the heart twice in each circuit.

  • Right side: body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs. Left side: lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.
  • Arteries: thick, elastic walls, high pressure. Veins: thin walls, valves, low pressure. Capillaries: one cell thick, for exchange.
  • Red blood cells carry oxygen; phagocytes engulf bacteria; lymphocytes make antibodies; platelets help clotting.
  • Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
Example

Heart rate 70, stroke volume 80 cm³. Cardiac output?

70 × 80 = 5600 cm³/min

Answer: 5.6 dm³/min

Example

Which vessel brings oxygenated blood to the heart?

from the lungs

Answer: pulmonary vein

Common mistakes

  • Saying all arteries carry oxygenated blood (not the pulmonary artery).
  • Saying the right ventricle has the thickest wall.
  • Saying veins have thick walls.
  • Mixing up phagocytes (engulf) and lymphocytes (antibodies).

faq.a: Blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit: once to the lungs (pulmonary circulation) and once to the rest of the body (systemic circulation).

faq.q: How are arteries different from veins?
faq.a: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure and have thick, muscular, elastic walls. Veins carry blood back at low pressure and have thinner walls, a wider lumen and valves.
Fatty deposits build up in the coronary arteries, narrowing them so less oxygen reaches the heart muscle. Smoking, a high-fat diet, lack of exercise and stress increase the risk.

items.q: Which chambers contract together to pump blood out of the heart into the arteries?
c: the right atrium and right ventricle
items.e: Ventricular systole.

items.q: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than that of the right ventricle?
c: It receives blood from the lungs.
It pumps blood at high pressure all round the body, not just to the nearby lungs.
items.e: Both ventricles pump the same volume.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 65 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 80 cm³. What is the cardiac output in dm³ per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 65 × 80 = 5200 cm³/min.

items.q: Why does lack of exercise increase the risk of coronary heart disease?
c: Nicotine and carbon monoxide damage artery walls and raise blood pressure.
It is linked to high blood pressure and obesity.
items.e: In coronary heart disease, the coronary arteries are narrowed by fatty deposits (atherosclerosis), so less oxygen reaches the heart muscle.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 80 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 cm³. What is the cardiac output in dm³ per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 80 × 70 = 5600 cm³/min.

items.q: Which part of the blood has this role: “transports dissolved glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide”?
items.e: Plasma: transports dissolved glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide.

items.q: Why does stress increase the risk of coronary heart disease?
c: It is linked to high blood pressure and obesity.
Fatty deposits build up in the coronary arteries.
items.e: In coronary heart disease, the coronary arteries are narrowed by fatty deposits (atherosclerosis), so less oxygen reaches the heart muscle.

items.q: Why does a diet high in saturated fat and cholesterol increase the risk of coronary heart disease?
c: Fatty deposits build up in the coronary arteries.
Nicotine and carbon monoxide damage artery walls and raise blood pressure.
It is linked to high blood pressure and obesity.
items.e: In coronary heart disease, the coronary arteries are narrowed by fatty deposits (atherosclerosis), so less oxygen reaches the heart muscle.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 150 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 100 cm³. What is the cardiac output in dm³ per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 150 × 100 = 15 000 cm³/min.

items.q: What causes the 'lub' sound of the heartbeat?
c: the closing of the bicuspid and tricuspid valves
the closing of the semilunar valves
items.e: 'Dub' is the semilunar valves closing.

items.q: What is the function of phagocytes?
c: transports dissolved glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide
items.e: Phagocytes: engulf and digest bacteria (phagocytosis).

items.q: Which part of the blood has this role: “carry oxygen as oxyhaemoglobin”?
items.e: Red blood cells: carry oxygen as oxyhaemoglobin.

items.q: What is meant by double circulation?
c: Blood is pumped twice per second.
Blood flows in two directions in each vessel.
Blood passes through the heart twice in each complete circuit of the body.
items.e: Pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation.

items.q: In the tissues, which way do the particles of oxygen move across the capillary walls?
c: it does not cross the capillary wall
from the blood to the cells
out of the capillaries at the arterial end
from the cells to the blood
items.e: Food and oxygen leave the blood for the cells; waste such as carbon dioxide and urea enters the blood. Tissue fluid forms from plasma at the arterial end.

items.q: What is the function of platelets?
items.e: Platelets: help the blood to clot.

items.q: Which part of the blood has this role: “help the blood to clot”?
items.e: Platelets: help the blood to clot.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 60 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 100 cm³. What is the cardiac output in dm³ per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 60 × 100 = 6000 cm³/min.

items.q: What is the role of the septum?
c: pumps oxygenated blood to the body through the aorta
receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava
stop blood flowing back from the arteries into the ventricles
items.e: The septum: separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

items.q: Which part of the heart has this role: “pumps oxygenated blood to the body through the aorta”?
items.e: The left ventricle: pumps oxygenated blood to the body through the aorta.

items.q: Which part of the heart has this role: “receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava”?
items.e: The right atrium: receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava.

items.q: What is tissue fluid?
c: plasma that has passed out through capillary walls and bathes the cells
items.e: It does not contain red blood cells or large proteins.

items.q: Blood enters the right atrium. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Blood enters the left atrium. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: What is the role of the right ventricle?
c: pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery
receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava
receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein
stop blood flowing back from the arteries into the ventricles
items.e: The right ventricle: pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery.

items.q: Blood enters the body organs. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Which part of the heart has this role: “pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery”?
items.e: The right ventricle: pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery.

items.q: Why do red blood cells have no nucleus?
c: They do not need to carry oxygen.
There is more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen.
items.e: They are also biconcave.

items.q: Blood is in the lungs. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: Which part of the heart has this role: “separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood”?
items.e: The septum: separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

items.q: What is the role of the right atrium?
c: receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein
pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery
receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava
items.e: The right atrium: receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava.

items.q: Why is the pulmonary artery unusual?
c: It carries oxygenated blood to the lungs.
It is an artery that carries deoxygenated blood.
It has valves along its length.
It carries blood to the heart.
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

items.q: Blood enters the lungs. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Which part of the heart has this role: “receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein”?
items.e: The left atrium: receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein.

items.q: Why do veins have valves?
c: to stop blood flowing backwards, as the pressure is low
items.e: Muscles squeeze veins and push blood towards the heart.

items.q: What is the role of the left ventricle?
c: pumps oxygenated blood to the body through the aorta
receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava
receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein
items.e: The left ventricle: pumps oxygenated blood to the body through the aorta.

items.q: Blood enters the vena cava. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Blood is in the aorta. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: Does the vena cava carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The vena cava carries deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.

items.q: Which blood vessels have thick, muscular, elastic walls and a narrow lumen?
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Why do capillaries have walls one cell thick?
c: They carry blood at high pressure away from the heart.
They allow exchange of substances with tissue cells.
They return blood at low pressure to the heart.
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Which structure is typical of capillaries?
c: thick, muscular, elastic walls and a narrow lumen
thin walls, a wide lumen and valves
items.e: Structure fits function: capillaries allow exchange of substances with tissue cells.

items.q: Does the pulmonary vein carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the left ventricle to the body?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Does the pulmonary artery carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

items.q: Which blood vessels have walls one cell thick?
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Why do arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls and a narrow lumen?
c: They return blood at low pressure to the heart.
They allow exchange of substances with tissue cells.
They carry blood at high pressure away from the heart.
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: What does haemoglobin combine with in the lungs?
items.e: Oxyhaemoglobin releases oxygen in the tissues.

items.q: What happens when a blood vessel is cut?
c: Platelets help to change soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads, which trap blood cells to form a clot.
Phagocytes form a scab by themselves.
items.e: The clot stops blood loss and entry of pathogens.

items.q: Blood enters the pulmonary vein. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Which blood vessels have thin walls, a wide lumen and valves?
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the body to the right atrium?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Does the renal artery carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The renal artery carries oxygenated blood from the aorta to the kidney.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: A student counts 36 pulse beats in 20 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
items.e: Heart rate = 36 × (60 ÷ 20).

items.q: A student counts 30 pulse beats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?

items.q: Blood is in the pulmonary vein. Where does it go next?

items.q: Why does high blood pressure increase the risk of coronary heart disease?
c: Nicotine and carbon monoxide damage artery walls and raise blood pressure.
It is linked to high blood pressure and obesity.
items.e: In coronary heart disease, the coronary arteries are narrowed by fatty deposits (atherosclerosis), so less oxygen reaches the heart muscle.

c: Fatty deposits build up in the coronary arteries.

items.e: Heart rate = 30 × (60 ÷ 20).

items.q: Capillaries are very narrow and have thin walls. Why is this useful?
c: Substances diffuse quickly between the blood and the cells over a short distance.
Blood flows quickly at high pressure.
items.e: Red blood cells pass in single file.

items.q: Why do people with fewer red blood cells (anaemia) feel tired?
c: Less oxygen is carried to the cells for respiration.
items.e: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin.

items.q: Which part of the heart has this role: “stop blood flowing back from the ventricles into the atria”?

items.q: Blood is in the left atrium. Where does it go next?

items.q: Blood leaves the heart from the left ventricle. Which route does it take to reach the lungs?
c: aorta → body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery
items.e: Double circulation.

items.q: What is the role of the left atrium?
c: pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs through the pulmonary artery
receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein
stop blood flowing back from the arteries into the ventricles
stop blood flowing back from the ventricles into the atria
items.e: The left atrium: receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein.

items.q: During exercise, the heart rate rises. Why?
c: More oxygen and glucose must reach the muscles for faster respiration, and more carbon dioxide must be removed.
The heart needs to cool down.
items.e: Cardiac output increases.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 75 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 65 cm³. What is the cardiac output in dm³ per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 75 × 65 = 4875 cm³/min.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 72 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 90 cm³. What is the cardiac output in dm³ per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 72 × 90 = 6480 cm³/min.

items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: A coronary artery becomes blocked. Why can this cause a heart attack?
c: Blood flows backwards into the lungs.
The heart muscle beyond the blockage gets no oxygen and glucose, so it cannot respire and dies.
The heart fills with too much blood.
items.e: Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle.

items.q: Which structure is typical of veins?
c: thick, muscular, elastic walls and a narrow lumen
thin walls, a wide lumen and valves
items.e: Structure fits function: veins return blood at low pressure to the heart.

items.q: A student counts 15 pulse beats in 10 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
items.e: Heart rate = 15 × (60 ÷ 10).

items.q: Why is a hole in the septum between the ventricles harmful?
c: Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix, so less oxygen reaches the body.
The heart beats faster than normal.
Blood cannot reach the lungs at all.
items.e: The septum keeps the two sides separate.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the aorta to the kidney?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Why does blood pressure fall as blood moves from arteries to veins?
c: Friction and the huge total cross-section of the capillaries slow it and reduce pressure.
Blood is lost at each organ.
items.e: Veins have valves and are squeezed by muscles.

items.q: What is the function of plasma?

items.e: Plasma: transports dissolved glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones and carbon dioxide.

items.q: Which change to lifestyle reduces the risk of coronary heart disease?
items.e: A balanced diet low in saturated fat also helps.
